name: Cucumber foot

card.summary: A historical Chinese foot-binding form from Sichuan that folded the toes under without distorting the heel or ankle, aiming for a smaller, more delicate foot.
card.note: Part of foot binding, a historical practice associated with infection, lifelong disability and deaths; ended in the 20th century.

quick.overview:
Cucumber foot (huangguajiao) is described as a less severe variant of Chinese foot binding found in Sichuan, in which the toes were folded under but the heel and ankle were not distorted. Binding as a whole aimed at a small, narrow foot, the ideal of which was the three-inch 'golden lotus'.

Foot binding was a mark of beauty, status and marriageability for women in China from roughly the Song dynasty until the early 20th century. Cucumber foot sits within that larger practice as one of the recognised shapes.
quick.how: This is a historical practice. Binding generally began in girlhood, with the foot wrapped tightly in bandages to reshape it over years; the cucumber form is described as folding the toes under without the heel and ankle deformation of other styles. The practice has been illegal in China since 1912 and is not carried out today.
quick.risks: Foot binding in general caused infection, gangrene and in some cases death, along with lifelong disability, broken bones and difficulty walking. The practice is documented as harmful and has ended.

lead: Cucumber foot (huangguajiao) is a term used for a less severe form of Chinese foot binding associated with Sichuan, in which the toes were folded under without distorting the heel or ankle.[1]

Foot binding sought to produce small, narrow feet that were admired as beautiful and associated with status and marriage prospects. Bound feet were graded by size, from the ideal three-inch 'golden lotus' through the larger 'silver lotus' and 'iron lotus'.[1] The cucumber foot is listed among the variants alongside northern and southern styles, which differed in how the foot was folded.[1]

The practice spread from the elite in the Song dynasty to lower classes by the Qing, and by the 19th century an estimated 40 to 50 percent of Chinese women had bound feet.[1] Campaigns and legal bans through the 19th and 20th centuries ended it.

angle.text: Binding produced a shortened foot that was prized in its time as a sign of beauty and refinement. The cucumber form is reported as a milder version that left the heel and ankle undistorted.

infobox: Toes folded under; heel and ankle not distorted

paras: Within foot binding terminology, the cucumber foot is described as a less severe Sichuan form that folded the toes under without distorting the heel or ankle.[1] Other categories described include the golden lotus (about three Chinese inches, roughly 11 cm), silver lotus (about 13 cm) and iron lotus (about 17 cm or larger), as well as northern styles with a large heel and small forefoot and southern styles that pulled the forefoot toward the heel.[1]

Accounts of origin vary, one linking it to dancers at the court of Li Yu in the 10th century; poems around 1100 appear to allude to it and the earliest archaeological evidence comes from tombs of the 13th century.[1] The practice spread among the Song elite and reached lower classes by the Qing; Manchu edicts against it in 1636, 1638 and 1664 failed.[1]
Anti-footbinding societies formed from 1874, the Republic of China banned it in 1912, and it had virtually disappeared by 1949, with the last new case reported in 1957.[1]

Binding often began between ages four and nine. Infection was the most common complication and could lead to gangrene and septic shock; the estimate given is that up to 10 percent of girls may have died, and survivors faced lifelong disability including fractures and muscle atrophy.[1] The sources describe the cucumber form as milder in deformity, but they do not give separate outcome figures for it.

timeline.event: One account links the origin of foot binding to dancers under Li Yu.[1]
Natural Foot Society formed in Xiamen.[1]
The Republic of China bans foot binding.[1]
